weekLabel: Week 8 · Meeting B · Project 1 Studio and Evidence Clinic

slides.title: Give a critique, pass one, and finish Project 1
slides.subtitle: Meeting B · peer-clinic protocol, a rubric-tied submission checklist, and structured studio time — no new library today
slides.teaching: Fall Break removed this week's Meeting A entirely; open by naming that plainly — today is entirely peer clinic and project-finishing time, and Project 1 is due at the end of this session.

slides.title: A partner is the cheapest grader you'll get
slides.statement: If a partner can't reproduce your numbers from a cold restart, an instructor won't be able to either.
slides.supporting: Today trades new content for a structured, rubric-tied peer critique, then studio time to fix what it finds — before you submit, not after.
slides.teaching: Say explicitly that no new library or concept is introduced today; every item on the checklist already came from Weeks 4-7.

outcomes.head: Critique
outcomes.body: Give and receive a structured, rubric-tied critique of a partner's data provenance and reproducibility.

outcomes.head: Audit
outcomes.body: Check your own Project 1 package, line by line, against the actual rubric before you submit it.

outcomes.head: Verify
outcomes.body: Confirm your pipeline runs cold — restarted kernel, top to bottom — with no manual fixes in between.

outcomes.head: Submit
outcomes.body: Turn in the complete package: two exact-schema CSVs, this week's figures and map, report, README, and AI-use disclosure.

slides.teaching: These are today's only outcomes — no new syntax is being taught, so hold the group to using class time on their own files, not on note-taking.

items: Confirm you're bringing all four Project 1 parts
Learn the peer-clinic protocol: swap, run cold, trace, note
Run the clinic against the actual rubric checklist
Studio time: fix, finalize, and submit
slides.teaching: Write the 46-minute studio-time block on the board now so students can see the whole session's shape before it starts.

slides.title: Confirm your four parts before the clinic starts
rows: Cleaned CSV (exact schema) + data dictionary + drop-justification memo
Grouped-summary CSV + IQR flags (z-score/merge optional extensions)
Part III — Two Purposeful Static Figures
Two static figures (fig/ax) — one shows a cleaning/outlier fix, one is annotated
Part IV — Choose One Evidence Extension
ONE chosen extension: map + metric (Wk 7) OR a captioned FuncAnimation .gif (Wk 6) — not both
slides.callout: Three image/gif exports total — two static figures plus your one chosen map or .gif — plus two exact-schema CSVs, a report, a README, and an AI-use disclosure appendix — that's the whole package.
slides.teaching: If any row is empty, that's today's first priority — the clinic still works on an incomplete draft, but say so to your partner before they start critiquing it.

slides.title: Reproducibility: a cold-restart test, not a compliment
slides.definition: A result is reproducible when a partner can restart your kernel, run your scripts top to bottom with no manual fixes, and get your exact numbers back — every reported value traceable to a raw row, not just a script that happens to run without an error.

example.head: Why it takes a partner
example.body: You already know your own story, so your own gaps are invisible to you. Hand a partner only your folder and README — if they reproduce your numbers cold, you're done; if not, you just found the fix before your grade depended on it.

slides.note: 'It ran without an error' is not the same claim as 'it reproduced the report.' A stale intermediate CSV, a hard-coded path, or a cell run out of order can all still hand back numbers that don't match — that gap is exactly what the clinic below is built to catch.
slides.teaching: Ask for a show of hands: who has restarted their kernel and run their own script top-to-bottom since finishing it? Expect fewer hands than you'd like — that gap is what today closes.

slides.title: Two partners, two row orders — same grouped numbers?
slides.code:
# same 6 rows, different input order
summary_a = rooms_a.groupby('zone')['energy_kwh_m2_yr'].mean()
summary_b = rooms_b.groupby('zone')['energy_kwh_m2_yr'].mean()
print(summary_a.equals(summary_b))
slides.question: What does .equals() print here?
options: True — groupby sorts by key, so input row order does not matter.
False — each result keeps the first-seen zone order.
False — float summation order changes the mean.
Only if both files were sorted first.
slides.why: True. groupby sorts its output by key, so both Series align by index and value despite different input row order.
slides.teaching: Take a vote. After a cold run, input row order is not a valid excuse for mismatched grouped results.

slides.title: The peer-clinic protocol, four moves

steps.label: SWAP
steps.head: Trade files, not context
steps.body: Hand your partner only what a grader would get: the folder, the README, the report. No verbal walkthrough yet.

steps.label: RUN
steps.head: Restart and run cold
steps.body: From a fresh kernel, run their scripts in order. Note the first place it breaks or a number doesn't match the report.

steps.label: TRACE
steps.head: Follow one number back
steps.body: Pick one reported number and trace it from the report to the grouped-summary CSV to the cleaned CSV to the raw data.

steps.label: NOTE
steps.head: Write one fixable note
steps.body: Not a compliment — one sentence naming the rubric line, the gap, and what would close it.

slides.teaching: Demonstrate the RUN step live on your own copy of the Radley Hall pipeline from Weeks 4-7 first, so students see a cold restart before doing it to a partner's real files.

slides.title: Giving vs. receiving a critique

left.head: Giving a critique
left.body: Point at the rubric line, not a vibe. Name the specific number, formula, or file that's off, not just a feeling that something's off. Name one gap and one thing that already works.

right.head: Receiving a critique
right.body: Ask one clarifying question before defending the choice. Write the note down even if you disagree — you decide later what to change, but you can't act on a note you didn't keep.

slides.teaching: Model both roles briefly with a volunteer's real file before pairs start — the giving/receiving asymmetry is the actual skill here, not the checklist itself.

slides.title: Rubric-tied critique checklist
columns: Ask your partner to show you
rows: Data provenance, cleaning, and exact-format exports
Run your Week 4 cleaning script from a restart; confirm the exported CSV matches the exact schema.
IQR flags appear and every flagged row has a keep/investigate/exclude sentence; z-score and a merged benchmark are optional extras, not required.
Two figures, one showing a cleaning/outlier consequence, one with a direct annotation.
Whichever the student picked — a map with a projected CRS, or a captioned FuncAnimation .gif — is present and correct, not both.
The closing paragraph names two real limitations, not just one plot's caption.
Code quality, reproducibility, and AI-use disclosure
Docstrings and type hints on every function, and a complete AI-use disclosure appendix.
slides.teaching: These six rows are copied directly from Project 1's own rubric (Section 4 of the semester plan) — tell students plainly that this is not a new checklist, it is the actual grading instrument.

slides.title: Reread the reprojection line before your partner does

parts.label: A new object
parts.body: Reprojected copy — zones_merged is untouched by this call.

parts.label: Still EPSG:4326
parts.body: Degrees — correct for storage, wrong for measuring area or length.

parts.label: Reprojects
parts.body: Returns a new GeoDataFrame in the CRS you name; never edits in place.

parts.label: Target CRS
parts.body: UTM zone 18N, in meters — required before .area or .length means anything.

slides.teaching: This is rubric line 4's exact check, one line at a time — point at chip 4 and ask a volunteer whether their own script reprojects before or after it computes .area. 'After' is the bug from Week 7's AI-audit exercise — the exact defect to look for in a partner's code today.

slides.title: Before you submit: the hygiene check
rows: Your Week 4, 5, 6, and 7 scripts, and both CSVs, are named and formatted exactly as each week's spec required
Your assert-based validation runs clean, top to bottom, from a just-restarted kernel
One suggestion accepted as-is, one modified, one rejected or independently verified — named specifically, not generically
slides.callout: A missing, incomplete, or fabricated AI-use disclosure caps this submission at 70%, regardless of technical quality.
slides.teaching: Say the 70% cap out loud and let it land — this is a compliance gate from the course grading framework (Section 1), not a suggestion.

slides.title: Peer Clinic: swap and critique
slides.prompt: Trade folders with a partner and run their Project 1 pipeline cold.
steps: Restart your partner's kernel and run every script top to bottom.
Work down the rubric checklist together, rubric line by rubric line.
Trace one reported number back to the raw data with them watching.
Give one specific, fixable note per rubric line — then swap roles.
slides.teaching: 12 minutes total for both directions — roughly 5-6 minutes per partner. Circulate and listen for vague notes such as 'looks fine' and redirect them to a specific rubric line.

slides.title: Checkpoint 1 · Make the working directory explicit
slides.statement: A reproducible project does not depend on whichever folder Spyder happened to remember.
slides.supporting: Use a project-relative path strategy, print the working folder once, and keep data/outputs in named subfolders.
slides.teaching: Optional pause point: students show their partner the one line that makes paths inspectable.

slides.title: Checkpoint 2 · Cold-run evidence
slides.callout: Record the cold-run result in the submission checklist.
slides.teaching: Require evidence, not 'it worked on my laptop.'

slides.title: Checkpoint 3 · State what one row means

left.head: UNIT OF ANALYSIS
left.body: Room, sensor interval, building, parcel, simulation run, or another explicit entity.

right.head: WHY IT MATTERS
right.body: Counts, averages, joins, and claims are wrong if the reader assumes a different row meaning.

slides.teaching: Students complete: 'One row represents…'

slides.title: Checkpoint 4 · Separate missingness from outliers
slides.callout: A missing value cannot be an IQR outlier because no numeric value exists to compare.
slides.teaching: Check the Project 1 evidence table has two separate columns.

slides.title: Checkpoint 5 · Report n_rows and n_measured
slides.definition: The number of non-missing observations used for a statistic. It may be smaller than the number of rows in the group.

example.head: Example
example.body: Zone North: n_rows=12, n_measured=10 for energy intensity. The mean uses 10—not 12.

slides.note: Never let a grouped mean imply that every row was measured.
slides.teaching: Students point to both denominators in their table or caption.

slides.title: Checkpoint 6 · Mean or median?
slides.question: Which summary better represents the typical room before the extreme case is resolved?
options: Median, with the extreme case reported separately
slides.why: The median is resistant to the extreme value. Keep the case visible and run a sensitivity comparison before any exclusion.
slides.teaching: The point is a defended choice, not a universal 'median is better' rule.

slides.title: Checkpoint 7 · Run an outlier sensitivity check

left.head: WITH THE CASE
left.body: Report the statistic and interpretation using every measured value.

right.head: WITHOUT THE CASE
right.body: Report the same statistic after a justified temporary exclusion. If the claim changes, say so.

slides.teaching: A robust claim should disclose when one row controls the conclusion.

slides.title: Checkpoint 8 · Figure 1 answers a distribution question
slides.prompt: Open the exported distribution figure at presentation size.
steps: Read the title without seeing the code.
Identify the typical range and any unusual cases.
Write one bounded sentence the figure supports.
slides.teaching: If the sentence cannot be written, the chart purpose is not yet clear.

slides.title: Checkpoint 9 · Figure 2 answers a relationship question
slides.prompt: Audit the relationship figure as evidence, not decoration.
steps: Name x, y, units, and each encoded group.
Annotate the case that changes the interpretation.
Avoid causal language unless the design supports it.
slides.teaching: Use 'associated with' for observational patterns.

slides.title: Checkpoint 10 · Map or animation: one extension only

left.head: MAP
left.body: State CRS, spatial operation, legend meaning, and what location adds to the claim.

right.head: ANIMATION
right.body: State what changes, what stays fixed, frame units, and what motion reveals beyond a static figure.

slides.teaching: An extension must qualify the evidence, not merely look impressive.

slides.title: Checkpoint 11 · Caption as a four-part argument

steps.label: HOW
steps.head: Name the method
steps.body: Summary, filter, CRS, or frame logic.

steps.label: LIMIT
steps.head: State uncertainty
steps.body: Missing rows, proxy, sampling, or scope.

slides.teaching: Read captions without showing the figures; they should still make sense.

slides.title: Checkpoint 12 · Visual accessibility

left.head: ON THE SLIDE
left.body: Legible labels · units · sufficient contrast · direct annotation · no color-only meaning

right.head: IN THE FILE
right.body: Descriptive alt text · reading order · concise source note · meaningful filename

slides.teaching: Ask a partner to describe the chart without relying on red/green vocabulary.

slides.title: Checkpoint 13 · Reproducibility log
slides.callout: A short log saves the reviewer from reverse-engineering your setup.
slides.teaching: This can live in 00_START_HERE or a submission README.

slides.title: Checkpoint 14 · Triage peer feedback

steps.label: CLARITY
steps.head: Evidence is hard to read
steps.body: Revise title, table, annotation, or caption.

steps.label: SCOPE
steps.head: Claim is too broad
steps.body: Narrow the language or add evidence.

steps.label: OPTIONAL
steps.head: Preference
steps.body: Adopt only if it strengthens the question.

slides.teaching: Not every comment is equal; prioritize correctness and evidence.

slides.title: Checkpoint 15 · Complete the AI-use record
slides.callout: The record evaluates judgment, not whether AI was used.
slides.teaching: Students should be able to connect every accepted suggestion to a verification step.

slides.title: Checkpoint 16 · Six-slide narrative rehearsal

steps.head: Trust
steps.body: Data, denominators, grouped evidence, outlier decision.

steps.head: Visual evidence
steps.body: Two static figures, then one extension.

slides.teaching: The title slide plus five numbered content slides equals six total.

slides.title: Checkpoint 17 · Run the submission validator
slides.output:
PASS: 14/14 checks
Submission package is ready for final human review.
slides.explainHead: A validator is a floor, not a grade
slides.explainBody: It checks required files, non-placeholder artifacts, readable tables/figures, and declared metadata. It cannot judge whether the architectural claim is meaningful.
slides.teaching: Fix every failing check, then perform the human evidence review on the next slide.

slides.title: Checkpoint 18 · Final evidence audit
rows: Does each number have a denominator and unit?
Does each figure answer a different question?
Does the recommendation match the evidence?
slides.callout: A technically valid package can still make an unsupported claim.
slides.teaching: Partners initial each row after a cold-run review.

slides.title: Checkpoint 19 · Submit only after a 60-second rehearsal
slides.statement: If the evidence story cannot be explained in one minute, the slide sequence is not yet doing enough work.
slides.supporting: Question → trustworthiness → grouped/outlier evidence → two figures → extension → bounded recommendation and limits.
slides.teaching: One partner times; the other notes the first point where the story becomes unclear.

slides.title: Studio time: fix, finalize, and submit
slides.prompt: The rest of today is independent project work time — use it.
steps: Resolve the specific notes your partner just gave you first.
Confirm both CSVs and all three image/gif exports (two figures + your chosen map or .gif) match the exact spec.
Proofread the 600-800-word evidence memo and the AI-use disclosure appendix.
Submit the complete package and stay ready for the short pin-up.
slides.teaching: This is the final 27-minute studio block in the 80-minute meeting: reserve it for actual independent (or still-paired) project work, with you circulating room to room. Announce the exact submission mechanism and the pin-up order now, then go quiet and work the room.

slides.title: Reproducible, or it isn't evidence
takeaways: A reproducibility critique is a cold restart-and-run test, not a compliment.
Every rubric line has one concrete, checkable question — use it before your partner does.
AI-use disclosure is a compliance gate: missing or fabricated caps the score at 70%, no matter how good the rest is.
Project 1 is due at the end of this session — submit the package and keep the pin-up ready.
slides.teaching: Close by asking each pair to name one thing they fixed because of their partner's note — make the critique's value visible before everyone leaves.
